findings.text: Post execve refresh and address space initialization for memory context identifiers are globally visible helpers that other scheduler parts can call when a task keeps an address space or when a new address space needs identifier state.

Deferred identifier maintenance runs in process context and leaves early when no user tasks remain or when no update is pending, otherwise it tries to shrink capacity and then rewrites per task assignments unless the mode still indicates per CPU operation which is treated as unexpected.

Slow identifier maintenance serializes with a mutex while the pending flag test uses a raw spinlock with interrupts disabled, and the hard interrupt work item only schedules the slow work without taking that spinlock because scheduling may nest inside runqueue locking and wakeup paths.

Fresh identifier state starts with cleared maximum and mode and user count and per CPU thresholds and deferred flag, with initialized spinlock and mutex and work items and user list, with allowed CPUs copied from the creating task and with the identifier mask cleared for every possible CPU.

Attribute changes bracketed by begin and end helpers require the owning runqueue lock to be already held and refresh the runqueue clock unless the caller asked to skip that step, while mixed high order flag bits are treated as unexpected.

The begin step records task and class and flags with queued and running status and current priority and invokes departure callbacks when leaving a class before removing the task from queueing or current execution, and the end step requeues and reselects as recorded with arrival callbacks on class change including promotion preemption or demotion reschedule and otherwise notifies the class of priority change.
The per CPU change context carries the affected task with its former class and flags and saved queued and running indications plus saved priority for later comparison during the matching end step.
A core scheduling cookie object holds only a reference count where a zero value at the task level denotes absence of any sharing association.

Cookie creation allocates a fresh object with count set to one and takes a matching global core reference, lookup with a present value increments the count and provides the same value, and release frees memory and drops the global reference only on the final decrement.

Cookie replacement runs under the task runqueue lock and warns when either old or new association exists without core scheduling being enabled, temporarily removes the task from core tracking when needed, swaps the stored value, readds queued tasks when the new value is present, and requests a reschedule when the task is on CPU while providing the prior value.

Inheritance clones the current association under the priority lock with interrupts preserved, fork clears the tree node and inherits from the creator, teardown drops the owned reference, and the internal setter orders an extra hold with swap and release to keep counts balanced.
Fork inheritance and teardown and process scoped sharing control for core scheduling are globally visible operations that other kernel parts can invoke.

Sharing control supports query of an opaque hashed identifier with a user pointer and supports creation and directional sharing toward or from the target, validating command and scope and address alignment and resolving a zero process identifier to the caller before applying to one thread or to every thread of a group.

Sharing requires active simultaneous multithreading scheduling support and read credential access to every affected task with group wide checks performed under the task list read lock before any update, and distinct failures signal missing support and bad arguments and unknown tasks and denied access and allocation failure.
Accounting exposes two indexed statistics for user mode and system mode with readable labels user and system and a count marking the end of the valid range.
Each accounting group embeds control group state plus a per CPU array of total usage counters and a per CPU array of detailed kernel statistics.

Task lookup resolves through task control group state with safe handling of empty inputs and parent lookup follows the embedded parent link, while the statically defined root group is backed by global kernel statistics and a global per CPU usage store.

Group creation provides the shared root state when no parent exists and otherwise allocates a zeroed object with per CPU usage and statistics areas and ordered cleanup on failure, while teardown releases both per CPU areas and the enclosing object.

Per CPU reads report user time as user plus nice and system time as system plus interrupt plus soft interrupt and total time from the usage counter with out of range indexes warning and yielding zero, while writes only accept zero as a reset and ignore resets targeting the global root.
Sixty four bit counter reads and writes take the target runqueue lock with interrupts disabled on narrow word builds to avoid torn accesses and run without that extra locking on wide word builds.

Total handlers sum per CPU values across all possible CPUs with separate views for total and user and system, per CPU handlers emit space separated values in CPU order followed by newline, the combined table adds a header row with labels and one row per CPU, and the statistics view aggregates execution time before scaling and conversion to clock ticks.

One adjustment variant copies user and system values directly, while the monotonic variant serializes on the history lock and filters non advancing totals and distributes runtime proportionally to observed shares with all runtime assigned to the populated side when either share is empty and with both outputs clamped to never move backward.

Monotonic adjustment holds the history spinlock with interrupts disabled across the read modify write of prior user and system totals so concurrent callers observe consistent and non decreasing outputs.

Legacy control files are named usage and usage_user and usage_sys and usage_percpu and usage_percpu_user and usage_percpu_sys and usage_all and stat, with reset support only on the total usage entry and sequential output on the per CPU and table and stat entries.
Charging execution time requires the target CPU runqueue lock to be already held and adds the delta to the per CPU total of the task group and every ancestor toward the root.

Field accounting adds the given value to the current CPU detailed counter of the task group and ancestors up to but excluding the global root so global kernel statistics stay untouched by group updates.
The accounting subsystem descriptor wires allocation and release callbacks with legacy file handlers and enables early initialization.
Charging and field accounting and deadline search and frequency hook management and time adjustment are globally visible helpers for use across scheduling and accounting paths.

Deadline search first accepts any free and allowed CPU when a candidate mask is supplied and filters by capacity when asymmetric capacity is active with fallback to the strongest unsuitable CPU when filtering empties the set, otherwise it accepts the earliest tracked CPU only when affinity allows and the task deadline precedes the tracked deadline.
A deadline task fits a CPU when scaled CPU capacity meets or exceeds task density after adjustment for bandwidth and capacity shift difference.
An invalid heap position is represented by negative one.

Each heap element stores a deadline with CPU number and heap position, and the container holds a raw spinlock with size and free CPU mask and element array with the earliest deadline kept at the front.
Deadline search treats a non empty heap with an absent best CPU as unexpected and warns while still proceeding with affinity and deadline checks.
Frequency hook publication and clearing use read copy update ordered store semantics on a per CPU pointer so readers can observe the hook without exclusive locking.
Hook installation warns and refuses when data or callback is missing or when a hook is already present for the CPU, leaving any existing association unchanged.
Update eligibility holds when the current CPU belongs to the policy CPU set or when cross CPU updates are allowed and a hook is currently published for the current CPU.
